newsitem.title: USA: U.S. surgeon convicted of changing drug lord's face.
newsitem.headline: U.S. surgeon convicted of changing drug lord's face.

text.p: A prominent Philadelphia plastic surgeon was convicted on Thursday of helping a notorious drug lord elude police by surgically altering his face and fingerprints.
Dr. Jose Castillo, 68, was found guilty on federal charges of harbouring a fugitive and obstructing justice.

Prosecutors said Castillo was the secret ally of Richie Ramos, a drug dealer who sold over $20 million in cocaine and ruled his turf by throwing a hand grenade into a police station and pulling out a rival's teeth with pliers.

After Ramos went on the run from federal drug charges, prosecutors said, Castillo performed a series of late-night operations to remove gunshot scars from the drug lord's face, remodel his nose, slice nearly 50 pounds of fat from his waist, and turn his fingerprints upside down.

"A new Richie Ramos emerged, one whom a policeman who watched him grow up from the age of eight wouldn't recognise if he walked by him on the street," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Kristin Hayes during closing arguments in the trial.
Ramos was caught 18 months later by investigators staking out his wife's car.

"I couldn't believe it when I saw him," testified James Moffit, a Philadelphia police detective. "He used to be roly- poly, like a snowman, and suddenly he looks like that," Moffit said, pointing toward prosecution photos of a fashionably slim Ramos.
Castillo acknowledged operating on Ramos, but only once -- to treat grease burns suffered during a barbecuing accident before Ramos became a fugitive.
Even though he had treated the Ramos family for years and once testified on behalf of Ramos' mother in a court case, Castillo denied knowing of any drug involvement by family members.

Defence attorney Marc Raspanti argued that Castillo's long history of treating poor immigrants for free made it entirely believable that the drug dealer could have come in for bandaging and left without the doctor asking any questions.
Ramos, serving 30 years in prison, said the doctor cut off his fingerpads, turned them upside down, and sewed them back on.
However, he fumbled in court when it came to identifying the accused, pointing to the defence attorney instead.
Fingerprint experts said that although Ramos's fingers were scarred, they were still easily identifiable.
Castillo, who has yet to be sentenced, faces five years in prison for each conviction, as well as the loss of his medical license. He plans to appeal.
